answer: I used garnet's current default calibration set (f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). I checked every 3-qubit chain whose two links are both CZ pairs. The best chain is QB11 - QB12 - QB7, with QB12 in the middle. The two IRB CZ fidelities are 0.99869 (QB12-QB11) and 0.99802 (QB12-QB7). Their product is 0.99671. The next best chains were QB11-QB12-QB17 and chains centred on QB11 (QB12-QB11-QB16, product about 0.9947) or QB20 (about 0.9934). Both were lower. I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit directly on QB11, QB12 and QB7. It puts all three qubits in superposition, applies CZ(QB12,QB11) and CZ(QB12,QB7), then rotates QB11 and QB7 back. That turns the CZ gates into CNOT-style links. It has exactly 2 CZ gates and measures all three qubits. I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots (job 01a160a3-7518-7101-80c9-c54abe54d685). The counts were 000:53, 011:53, 100:50, 111:44. These counts are not a GHZ result. On a perfect machine you would see only 000 and 111, about half each. The mock returns counts that ignore the circuit, so they say nothing about the quality of the chain. Only a real garnet run would show how close the chain gets to GHZ. The principle is that CZ gates are noisy and every one adds error. Picking the pair of links with the best fidelity gives the cleanest entangled state. The job returned no circuit payload, so cz_count and measured qubits come from the circuit I submitted, not a server read-back.
